lead.headline: Acorn saved again as Olivetti raises its stake to 78.9%
body: Acorn has been saved from liquidation by a complex financial restructuring, according to the August 1 issue of Popular Computing Weekly. The magazine describes the arrangement as the BBC Micro maker’s second rescue package of the year, with Olivetti increasing its stake to 78.9 percent.

For households and classrooms already invested in the BBC Micro, the immediate importance is continuity. A computer system is more than its keyboard: owners depend on an ongoing supply of software, peripherals and support. The rescue keeps the company behind that system in the picture, without settling every question about its future.

The magazine’s cover links the rescue to new BBC micros. Its exhibition report also looks back at the preceding week’s Acorn User Exhibition at London’s Barbican, where the 32016 processor and BBC B Plus drew attention. Those previews should not be mistaken for fresh launches during this week.

Olivetti’s enlarged holding makes the Italian company still more central to Acorn’s prospects. The available report establishes the rescue and ownership percentage, not a precise signing date, cash injection or staffing settlement. For now, the week’s decisive news is that Acorn has another chance.
lead.dek: BBC Micro maker avoids liquidation in its second rescue package of the year.

stories.headline: The Way of the Exploding Fist earns its five stars
body: Melbourne House’s Commodore 64 karate game earns five stars in August’s Your Computer. At £9.95, The Way of the Exploding Fist offers 18 joystick-controlled blows, jumps, blocks and kicks, with either computer opposition or a second human at the controls.

Four background scenes frame the contests, while progressively ranked Dan opponents give solitary players a ladder to climb. This is a contemporary review, not evidence that the game first went on sale during July 29-August 4.

Programmer Gregg Barnett tells the magazine that making the computer play intelligently was the hardest task. The report describes 72-pixel-high fighters assembled from nine sprites apiece and 740 sprite shapes for their moves. BBC computers linked to Commodore 64s served as development equipment.

The magazine credits Greg Holland with music and reports separate 3K allocations for music and digitised vocal effects. Those are the contemporary account’s figures. The result brings animation, timing and a recognisable martial-arts contest together on a familiar home machine.

stories.headline: HomePak brings three jobs to one disk
body: Sheldon Leemon’s July COMPUTE! review examines a $49.95 package that combines HomeText writing, HomeFind filing and HomeTerm telecommunications. Russ Wetmore’s HomePak is reviewed for Atari machines with at least 48K and a disk drive, and for the Commodore 64 with disk drive.

The communications module supplies an online timer, XMODEM transfers, keyboard macros and an outgoing edit window. These are practical tools when connection time costs money. On Atari, roughly 7K buffers in HomeText and HomeTerm show the compromises involved in squeezing several jobs into an 8-bit computer.

The reviewed programs are not copy-protected. Buyers should nevertheless check versions: the review says the initial Commodore release cannot dial the 1650 modem and reports a free update. IBM PC, enhanced PCjr and Macintosh editions are forthcoming; the quoted $69.95 Macintosh price is not proof of present availability.

stories.headline: WordStar heads for the Amstrad CPC
body: MicroPro has announced plans to launch WordStar for the Amstrad CPC 464 and 664, Popular Computing Weekly reports on August 1. A familiar word-processing name is thus being directed toward machines often associated with the home and hobby desk.

The announcement is not a confirmed shipment. No verified price, retail date, memory requirement or bundled spelling checker accompanies the available report. Prospective buyers have a product to watch, not a complete purchase specification.

market.headline: Owners need continuity as well as new machines
market.summary: Acorn’s second rescue highlights the business behind the home-computer shelf. Meanwhile the August 1 press compares the preceding week’s Amiga unveiling with Atari ST, as established 8-bit owners weigh practical software and modem purchases.

worldAnchor.headline: Challenger reaches orbit after main-engine shutdown
worldAnchor.summary: Challenger launched July 29 at 5 p.m. EDT. A main engine shut down 5 minutes 45 seconds into ascent, requiring an abort-to-orbit maneuver; the seven-person crew carried the Spacelab-2 science payload.

bbsNote.headline: Typing time is money on commercial online services
bbsNote.summary: COMPUTE! July p.88, Arlan R. Levitan’s Saving Money With E-Mail, explains connect-time billing and long-distance costs even on free BBSs; HomeTerm’s timer and offline text handling provide a practical companion. Posts below are editorial summaries of printed reporting, not fabricated historical BBS messages.

posts.text: Levitan notes that spending 15 minutes entering a long message can cost a couple of dollars; composing before connecting avoids paying while thinking and typing. This is illustrative cost commentary, not a universal service tariff.
HomePak’s communications module includes an online timer, XMODEM transfer support and an edit window that sends a composed line when RETURN is pressed.
Your Computer August announces a planned commercial MUD with £20 joining cost and more than 100 simultaneous players claimed. It is an announced service, not a verified launch in this week.

curiosity.headline: A toy robot that sings to the wastepaper basket
curiosity.summary: Fred D’Ignazio’s July COMPUTE! column treats personality, not useful chores, as home robotics’ selling point.
curiosity.detail: Here Come the Toy Robots!, p.83, describes HEROjr singing Old MacDonald Has a Robot to a wastepaper basket; Maxx Steele stands two feet tall with a 150-word vocabulary and 20 prerecorded phrases; Tomy’s remote-controlled Omnibot 2000 is quoted at about $500. These are July magazine observations and Toy Fair previews for fall, not launches this week.

gadgetWatch.headline: High-speed twin-cassette decks face copyright ruling
gadgetWatch.summary: August’s Your Computer reports Mr Justice Whitford’s ruling against Amstrad over twin-cassette decks capable of copying prerecorded tapes. Amstrad intends to appeal the ruling.

undergroundDesk.headline: The Cracker’s memoir reaches the hobbyist press
body: August’s Your Computer notices Out of the Inner Circle, Bill Landreth’s Penguin book. The magazine identifies Landreth as The Cracker and says he wrote it while on probation after the FBI caught him accessing Telemail.

This is a contemporary book notice recalling earlier events, not a new arrest this week. The named handle belongs to the author; the report does not establish an additional crew. The story concerns the scene and its consequences, not instructions for entering somebody else’s computer.
undergroundDesk.dek: A book notice recalls an earlier collision between teenage computing and federal investigators.
